description: Hi, We're Outliers, an international team combining software development, UI/UX, and data engineering to build something meaningful with NASA data. If you're collaborative, committed, and excited about space exploration, we'd love to have you on board!
summary:
At the Moon’s south pole, low Sun angles and rugged terrain make sunlight and direct-to-Earth visibility highly dependent on location and time. Team Outliers developed Lunar Landing Site Navigator (Mission Atlas), an interactive web application that helps users explore and compare four candidate landing sites using NASA lunar terrain data and scientifically computed Sun and Earth positions.

Our Python-based scientific pipeline combines LOLA-derived elevation models, terrain-horizon calculations, and NASA/JPL SPICE ephemerides to estimate sunlight availability, Earth line of sight, and periods when both conditions occur together.

The application brings these results into an intuitive experience featuring interactive 3D lunar terrain, a Moon globe, visibility timelines, local-horizon visualizations, and synchronized comparisons across four sites.

For the November 14–December 14, 2026 scenario, our analysis identifies an approximately 12-day, 13-hour, 41-minute interval during which none of the four sites has direct Earth line of sight.

By making complex lunar data understandable and explorable, Mission Atlas supports educational exploration and preliminary mission-planning analysis while clearly communicating its scientific assumptions and limitations.
details:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator — Mission Atlas

Team Outliers | NASA International Space Apps Challenge 2026

The Challenge

Selecting a landing site near the Moon's south pole requires understanding more than surface geography. The Sun stays close to the horizon, and surrounding ridges and crater walls can obstruct sunlight for extended periods. The apparent direction of Earth also changes relative to the local terrain, creating important constraints on direct-to-Earth communication opportunities.

A location with favorable sunlight may not offer equally favorable Earth visibility. These conditions vary between sites and throughout time, making it difficult to compare candidate locations using terrain maps or celestial-position data alone.

Our goal was to make these relationships easier to explore, understand, and compare.

Our Solution

We developed Lunar Landing Site Navigator (Mission Atlas), an interactive scientific web application that combines authentic lunar terrain, calculated Sun and Earth positions, and terrain-aware visibility analysis.

The application examines four candidate locations near the lunar south pole:

  • Site 01 — Connecting ridge
  • Site 04 — Shackleton rim
  • Site 07 — Peak near Shackleton
  • Site 11 — de Gerlache rim

Users can explore each site's 3D terrain, navigate through a 30-day analysis period, examine the Sun and Earth relative to the local terrain horizon, and compare visibility conditions across all four locations.

Mission Atlas provides four connected experiences:

Explore: Interactive 3D terrain, a shared UTC clock, live condition readouts, local sky panoramas, and sunlight/Earth-visibility timelines.

Compare Sites: Synchronized four-site visibility windows, individual and shared visibility gaps, duration comparisons, and quantitative metrics.

Moon Globe: A contextual lunar globe showing the geographic positions of the candidate sites, with access to their detailed terrain views.

Method & Data: An accessible explanation of the scientific pipeline, NASA datasets, validation results, uncertainty, model assumptions, and data provenance.

Scientific Methodology

Our scientific calculations are performed in Python and exported as validated datasets for the web application.

1. Lunar terrain processing

We use NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) elevation data, including high-resolution lunar south-pole terrain products from NASA's Planetary Geodesy Data Archive. Terrain coverage combines approximately 5 m local elevation data with coarser 80 m and 240 m mosaics for more distant surroundings.

2. Local terrain horizons

For each selected landing point, the pipeline examines surrounding terrain in thousands of azimuth directions to determine the highest obstructing horizon angle. The calculation accounts for the Moon's curvature and uses a modeled observer height of 1 m above the surface.

3. Sun and Earth positions

NASA/JPL SPICE ephemerides, using the DE421-compatible lunar reference frame, provide the apparent directions of the Sun and Earth at each observation time.

4. Visibility analysis

The scientific model compares the celestial geometry with the local terrain horizon.

  • Sunlight is classified as available when at least 80% of the modeled solar disc is visible.
  • Earth line of sight is available when Earth's centre is above the local terrain horizon.
  • Joint visibility identifies periods when both conditions are satisfied.

The analysis produces time-dependent samples, visibility windows, transition events, and comparison metrics.

5. Interactive visualization

The scientific outputs are exported as JSON and presented through a React-based application. The frontend displays the precomputed scientific results rather than independently recalculating the physics. This separates the verified numerical pipeline from the interactive presentation layer.

Results and Key Findings

Our primary demonstration analyzes November 14 to December 14, 2026 (UTC).

The four sites exhibit similarly high modeled sunlight availability during this particular period. Sites 01, 07, and 11 meet the 80% solar-disc threshold throughout the analyzed interval, while Site 04 meets it for approximately 98.5% of the period.

Earth visibility varies more substantially:

  • Site 01: 46.8% of the period
  • Site 04: 37.3%
  • Site 07: 42.2%
  • Site 11: 48.9%

Site 11 has the highest modeled Earth line-of-sight availability in this scenario, but that does not make it the best overall landing location.

A particularly important finding is a shared interval of approximately 12 days, 13 hours, and 41 minutes, from December 1 at 02:18 UTC to December 13 at 15:59 UTC, during which none of the four analyzed sites has direct Earth line of sight.

This demonstrates why comparing sites on a synchronized timeline can reveal operational constraints that are difficult to recognize when examining individual locations separately.

Validation and Scientific Transparency

We conducted multiple checks to assess the numerical implementation.

An independent comparison of Sun and Earth directional geometry against JPL Horizons found a maximum reported angular difference of approximately 0.000011° across the tested locations and dates.

The released terrain-horizon profiles were also tested for sensitivity to finer sampling. All four released profiles meet the team's 0.01° sampling-convergence target.

The mathematical implementation was documented through a formula audit connecting the modeled equations to source code and tests.

These checks establish consistency between important parts of the implementation and their references. They do not establish that the physical predictions are free from terrain-data uncertainty.

Limitations

Mission Atlas is a research and educational prototype, not a flight-certified landing-site selection system.

The reported results apply to four specific points over one 30-day scenario. The model uses a 1 m observer height and simplified geometric assumptions. Direct Earth visibility represents geometric line of sight, not a guaranteed radio connection or communications link budget.

Terrain uncertainty remains significant. For a subset of high-resolution terrain blockers, estimated angular horizon uncertainty is approximately 0.02°–0.24°. This uncertainty has not been propagated into confidence intervals for the reported event times.

The application does not currently model comprehensive landing hazards, local surface slope and roughness, boulder distributions, thermal behavior, dust, radiation, or complete spacecraft power and communications systems.

The 3D terrain visualization uses synthetic hillshade lighting, clearly distinguished from the calculated sunlight conditions.

Technology and Implementation

The application uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and Three.js/React Three Fiber for the interactive frontend and lunar terrain visualization.

The scientific pipeline uses Python, numerical processing, NASA LOLA elevation datasets, and NASA/JPL SPICE geometry. Precomputed JSON scenarios connect the scientific analysis to the browser interface, allowing the project to operate as a statically deployed application without a live scientific-computation server.

The final web application is deployed using Cloudflare Pages, and the project source code is maintained on GitHub.

Impact and Future Development

Mission Atlas makes complex lunar exploration data more understandable to students, researchers, mission designers, and the broader public.

It demonstrates how open NASA datasets can be transformed into accessible tools that connect terrain, celestial geometry, and time-dependent exploration constraints.

The scientific approach is designed to support additional locations, although only four south-pole sites have been processed and demonstrated in this release.

Future development could expand geographic and temporal coverage, propagate terrain uncertainty into event-time estimates, incorporate more landing-safety criteria, and introduce detailed solar-power and communications models.

Our contribution is not to declare one landing site universally best, but to make the evidence and trade-offs behind lunar-site comparisons visible, interactive, and understandable.
